title: Tăng trưởng và tài nguyên · Problems / Solutions
prompt: Some societies are considering requiring governments to limit material consumption even if economic growth slows. What problems could this create, and what measures could be taken to address them?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Đề yêu cầu những vấn đề chính sách có thể tạo ra và biện pháp xử lý. Mỗi giải pháp phải thay đổi nguyên nhân của vấn đề cụ thể, nêu chủ thể thực hiện và cách biết hỗ trợ đã đến người hoặc tình huống chịu ảnh hưởng. Trường hợp này: Tuổi thọ sản phẩm dài làm giảm số chu kỳ khai thác, sản xuất và vận tải trên cùng lượng dịch vụ sử dụng. Máy giặt sửa được minh họa giảm nhu cầu vật liệu từ gốc, khác với xử lý sau khi thành rác. Giảm doanh số đột ngột làm lao động chịu chi phí chuyển đổi. Hỗ trợ chuyển nghề và phân biệt nhu cầu thiết yếu với thay mới tránh dùng mục tiêu môi trường để bỏ qua phân phối tổn thất.

paragraphs: Limiting material consumption can trigger rapid job losses in industries built on frequent replacement purchases, while a uniform reduction target can deny poorer households essential goods. A fair response must phase change around workers' real employment options and households' basic needs, rather than equate every reduction in purchases with an improvement in welfare.

Abrupt restrictions can threaten employment in industries that depend on high sales volumes. Firms built around frequent replacement purchases may respond to falling demand by cutting employment before workers can move elsewhere. An environmental gain can therefore create concentrated local losses, especially where the same industry supports many neighbouring businesses. Keeping a washing machine in service reduces replacement demand, whereas denying a first essential appliance to a low-income household raises a different question of fairness.

Transition plans should support workers and distinguish essential consumption from avoidable waste. Transition support should begin before production contracts, matching retraining to identifiable jobs in repair or other growing activities rather than promising that new work will appear automatically. Worker support should connect declining activities with viable new roles, while exemptions for essential needs prevent a uniform consumption target from worsening deprivation. Household rules should distinguish repeated discretionary upgrades from first access to necessities, so reducing waste does not become an instruction for poorer residents to remain deprived. Monitoring should follow the earnings and stability of workers who retrain, since completion of a course alone does not establish that a displaced household has regained a sustainable income. Progress should be measured by material use per useful service and by workers' transition prospects, rather than by lower sales figures alone.
Growth in replacement sales is a weak measure of welfare when durable products meet the same needs with less extraction; the transition remains defensible only if its costs are shared fairly.
